Important Note on Data By Strength Class: 

To model the embodied carbon of concrete by strength class, assumptions need to be made on cement content per unit volume of concrete. These vary considerable, even at the same specified strength class. More cement is also often added into a mixture, e.g. to cure quicker, than is needed to reach the stated strength class.
 
The data below has been modelled using the ICE Cement, Mortar, Concrete model with an estimate of realistic cement contents, not minimum cement contents. The use of lower carbon cement replacements also influences the total cementitious content, e.g. if using PFA or GGBS, often the total cementitious content is increased over a CEM I mixture.

This adds additional uncertainty to this data by strength class. There is no substitute for finding out the actual cement content used in a mixture (not specified min cement content - actual cement content used by the contractor). The cement content for your mixture at this strength class might be a very different value than assumed here. It is worth finding out more details on actual cement content.

Category:
The data in this section includes the carbon stored in the timber. Carbon storage can only be claimed for sustainably sourced timber. The data in this section is more aligned with how most EPDs have been reporting the carbon footprint of timber. However, users should be aware that the end of life (EOL) stage for timber is particularly important. 

The amount of stored carbon will be given back to the atmosphere. The amount given back depends upon the EOL route, such as incineration, landfill, recycling or reuse. If including carbon storage in calculations for Modules A1-3, it is particularly important to also model the EOL impacts. 

The carbon storage values are presented as negative in magnitude (-, minus). To provide an example, if -1.5 kg CO2 is stored per kg of wood, and 0.5 kgCO2e is the embodied carbon of a wood (Mod A1-3) without carbon storage. Then the embodied carbon with carbon storage, in this example, would be -1.0 kg CO2e per kg of wood. 

Embodied carbon data with carbon storage is typically a negative in magnitude number and therefore must be used with care. Carbon storage can only be applied to timber that ends up in a product - not to excess timber that will become waste material. It is also vital that the end of life stage is considered.
